The Trump administration proposed higher tariffs on goods from China and the EU. US equities were mixed: the Nasdaq 100 fell approximately 2.1%, the S&P 500 dropped 0.6%, while the Dow edged up 0.1%. December corn rose approximately 1.3% to 456 cents; wheat eased 0.8% to 584 cents; January soybeans edged up to 1,236 cents. Newcastle coal eased to $145. Markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving. OPEC+ meets Saturday November 29.

overview: Wednesday's session delivered a dramatic divergence between commodities and crude oil. Gold broke below $3,500 per ounce for the first time since September 2025, settling approximately 2.5% lower at $3,474 — the twelfth decline in thirteen sessions — after the October PCE report (headline 3.8%, core 3.3%) reinforced December rate-hike expectations at 97.8% per CME FedWatch. Silver fell approximately 4.9% to $39. The LME base metals rout deepened: tin plunged 7.2% to $36,710 — a one-year low — copper slipped below $12,000 per tonne to an 11-month trough at $11,596 ($5.26 per pound), and zinc eased 1.5% to $3,389. Platinum dropped roughly 4.5% to $1,200; palladium fell 3.1% to $843. Oil was the standout: Brent initially fell to approximately $87 on supply-surplus fears before staging a dramatic reversal to $94 — up 3.3% from Tuesday — after IRGC mines struck two more tankers and an LNG carrier in the Strait of Hormuz. WTI rose to $84. The Trump administration proposed higher tariffs on goods from China and the EU, adding to the dollar's strength. US equities were mixed — the Nasdaq 100 fell roughly 2.1%, the S&P 500 dropped 0.6%, while the Dow edged up 0.1% on defensive rotation. Bitcoin fell below $60,000 to approximately $58,500; Ethereum dropped to $1,640.

China announced a two-month extension of its US-specific export-control suspension on gallium, germanium and antimony, pushing the deadline from November 27 to January 27, 2027 — removing an immediate supply cliff risk for Western semiconductor and defence supply chains. Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority added 26 tugboats to its vessel blacklist, bringing the total to 266 vessels listed for transiting without Tehran's permission — analysts said the move aims to deny salvage and firefighting services to attacked vessels, further raising the cost and risk of Hormuz transit. OPEC+ ministers meet Saturday November 29 to decide 2027 output policy amid a tightening supply backdrop. December corn rose approximately 1.3% to 456 cents per bushel; wheat eased 0.8% to 584 cents; January soybeans edged up to 1,236 cents — grains were mixed in pre-Thanksgiving holiday trade. Newcastle coal eased to $145. The October PCE readings — headline 3.8%, core 3.3% — were broadly in line with expectations but left little room for the Fed to soften its hawkish stance. Q3 GDP was revised to 4.3% annualised; initial jobless claims fell to 189,000. Markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving. The Fear and Greed Index remains in extreme fear territory.

watchItems.title: Brent stages dramatic reversal from $87 to $94 as new IRGC mine attacks strike two tankers and an LNG carrier in Hormuz
watchItems.text: Brent crude staged a dramatic intraday reversal on Wednesday, initially falling to approximately $87 on supply-surplus fears before surging to $94 — up 3.3% — after IRGC mines struck two more tankers and an LNG carrier in the Strait of Hormuz. This follows Tuesday's attack on four tankers. Goldman Sachs's December forecast of $105 and $140 risk scenario remain in play. Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority added 26 tugboats to its vessel blacklist, bringing the total to 266 vessels listed for transiting without Tehran's permission — a move analysts said aims to deny salvage and firefighting services to attacked vessels. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Gulf. OPEC+ ministers meet Saturday November 29 to decide 2027 output policy. The oil rally despite broad commodity selling underscores how supply-side geopolitical risk continues to dominate crude pricing.

watchItems.title: Gold breaks below $3,500 to 15-month low as October PCE reinforces December rate-hike expectations at 97.8%
watchItems.text: COMEX gold settled approximately 2.5% lower at $3,474 on Wednesday, breaking below $3,500 for the first time since September 2025. This marks the twelfth decline in thirteen sessions. The October PCE report — headline 3.8%, core 3.3% — reinforced December rate-hike expectations, now priced at 97.8% per CME FedWatch. The dollar strengthened further, and the Trump administration's proposal for higher tariffs on China and the EU added to bullion's headwinds. Silver fell 4.9% to $39. Platinum dropped 4.5% to $1,200. Gold has fallen approximately 9% over the past week and over 6% in November, on track for a third straight monthly decline. Key support at $3,400; resistance at $3,500. Traders see little prospect of relief before the December 9-10 FOMC meeting.

watchItems.title: China extends gallium, germanium and antimony export-control suspension by two months to January 27, 2027
watchItems.text: China announced a two-month extension of its US-specific export-control suspension on gallium, germanium and antimony, pushing the deadline from November 27, 2026 to January 27, 2027. The extension removes an immediate supply cliff risk for Western semiconductor and defence supply chains. Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China versus approximately $460 domestically — a roughly 4.5x premium. The extension follows similar rolling extensions that have effectively maintained a trade truce with Washington. However, the underlying licensing regimes remain in force during the suspension, and market participants note the two-month window is short enough to maintain strategic leverage. China produces approximately 99% of global gallium and 60-80% of germanium. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery has taken FID but is not yet producing.

watchItems.title: LME base metals rout deepens — tin plunges 7.2% to one-year low, copper at 11-month trough as November slide reaches 18%
watchItems.text: The LME base metals complex deepened its November rout on Wednesday with tin plunging 7.2% to $36,710 per tonne — its lowest level in a year — and copper slipping below $12,000 per tonne to an 11-month low at $11,596 ($5.26 per pound). LME copper has now fallen approximately 18% in November. Shanghai tin fell as much as 9.6% intraday. Zinc eased 1.5% to $3,389. Aluminium fell 0.7% to $2,750. Drivers include dollar strength, the October PCE data, the Trump administration's tariff proposals on China and the EU, and continued concern over slowing AI-related spending after the tech sell-off. Nickel bucked the trend, edging up 0.5% to $15,175 after touching a one-year low. Markets are closed Thursday for Thanksgiving. OPEC+ meets Saturday.

desk.name: Gold
desk.m: COMEX settle ~$3,474 -2.47% · broke below $3,500 — 15-month low · 12th decline in 13 sessions · Oct PCE 3.8%/core 3.3% · Dec hike 97.8% · Trump tariffs on China/EU
desk.sum: Gold broke below $3,500 per ounce for the first time since September 2025 on Wednesday, with COMEX December futures settling approximately 2.47% lower at $3,474 — the twelfth decline in thirteen sessions. The October PCE report (headline 3.8%, core 3.3%) reinforced December rate-hike expectations, now priced at 97.8% per CME FedWatch. The dollar strengthened further, and the Trump administration's proposal for higher tariffs on China and the EU added to bullion's headwinds. Gold fell as low as $3,469 intraday before a slight recovery into the close. Gold has fallen approximately 9% over the past week and over 6% in November — on track for a third straight monthly decline. Key support at $3,400; resistance at $3,500.

desk.name: Silver
desk.m: New 52-week low · down ~26% in Nov · gold-silver ratio widened to ~89 · dollar strength intensifies · higher beta amplified losses
desk.sum: Silver fell approximately 4.9% to $39 per ounce on Wednesday, extending its rout alongside gold as the October PCE data reinforced December rate-hike expectations. Silver's higher beta to gold amplified the downside — the gold-silver ratio widened to approximately 89. Silver has now fallen approximately 26% in November, far outpacing gold's 6% decline for the month. The industrial metal is down more than 22% year on year. The dollar's continued advance and the Trump administration's tariff proposals on China and the EU add further headwinds. Key support at $38; resistance at $41.

desk.name: Oil
desk.m: WTI $84 · dramatic reversal: fell to $87 on surplus fears, surged to $94 on new IRGC mine attacks — 2 tankers + LNG carrier · Iran blacklists 26 tugboats · Goldman: $105 Dec, $140 risk · OPEC+ Nov 29
desk.sum: Brent crude staged a dramatic intraday reversal on Wednesday, initially falling to approximately $87 on supply-surplus fears before surging to $94 — up 3.3% from Tuesday — after IRGC mines struck two more tankers and an LNG carrier in the Strait of Hormuz. WTI rose to $84. This follows Tuesday's attack on four tankers. Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority added 26 tugboats to its vessel blacklist, bringing the total to 266 — aiming to deny salvage services to attacked vessels. Goldman Sachs's December forecast of $105 and $140 risk scenario remain operative. The reversal from broad risk-off selling underscores how Hormuz supply disruption continues to dominate crude pricing. OPEC+ meets Saturday November 29.
desk.src: Reuters · Trading Economics · Goldman Sachs · Insurance Journal

desk.name: Copper
desk.m: LME $11,596/t · below $12,000 — 11-month low · down 18% in Nov · tariff fears · AI sell-off continues · Shanghai copper -6.3%
desk.sum: Copper slipped below $12,000 per tonne to an 11-month low at $11,596 ($5.26 per pound LME) on Wednesday, deepening the November rout to approximately 18%. The sell-off was driven by dollar strength after the October PCE data, the Trump administration's tariff proposals on China and the EU, and continued concern over slowing AI-related spending. Shanghai's most-traded copper contract fell 6.3%. Copper is now approximately 22% below its September record. Despite tight physical conditions and record Yangshan premiums, macro headwinds dominate near-term pricing. Key support at $5.15/lb ($11,350/t).

desk.name: Coal
desk.m: Continued easing from $147 · Brent reversal to $94 mixed signal · LNG supply crisis intact · still up ~36% YTD · Thanksgiving thin trade · OPEC+ Nov 29
desk.sum: Newcastle coal eased approximately 1.4% to $145 per tonne on Wednesday, continuing its gradual retreat from recent highs. While Brent crude reversed sharply to $94 on new Hormuz mine attacks — supportive for coal-to-gas substitution economics — the broader risk-off mood and weaker industrial commodity sentiment weighed. Coal remains up approximately 36% year to date. QatarEnergy's force majeure continues through at least end-December 2026. Markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving, thinning liquidity. OPEC+ meets Saturday.

desk.name: Platinum
desk.m: 15-month low alongside gold · dollar strength intensifies · down ~10% in Nov · thin market amplifying moves · South African supply still constrained
desk.sum: Platinum dropped approximately 4.5% to $1,200 per ounce on Wednesday, tracking gold below $3,500 as the October PCE data reinforced rate-hike expectations. Platinum is at its lowest level since August 2025. The thin market continues to amplify moves in both directions. South African mine supply remains constrained, and hydrogen electrolysis demand provides structural long-term support, but the dollar's advance and tariff fears dominate near-term. Platinum has fallen approximately 10% in November. Key support at $1,175; resistance at $1,230.

desk.name: Palladium
desk.m: Well below $900 · EV transition headwind dominant · dollar strength intensifies · down ~40% YoY · structurally challenged
desk.sum: Palladium fell 3.1% to approximately $843 per ounce on Wednesday, moving further below the $900 level. The decline was driven by the dollar's continued advance and the broader precious metals sell-off. Palladium's structural headwind from the EV transition continues to cap rallies. Down approximately 40% year on year. The pattern of failing to hold $900 reflects the metal's fundamental weakness. Key support at $820; resistance at $870.

desk.name: Hormuz Terminal
desk.m: IRGC mines struck 2 more tankers + LNG carrier · Iran blacklists 26 tugboats — 266 total · denying salvage services · Brent reversed to $94 · Goldman: $105 Dec, $140 risk · 3 US carriers · OPEC+ Nov 29
desk.sum: IRGC mines struck two more tankers and an LNG carrier in the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, following Tuesday's attack on four tankers. Brent crude reversed sharply from $87 to $94 on the news. Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority added 26 tugboats to its vessel blacklist, bringing the total to 266 vessels for transiting without Tehran's permission — analysts said the move aims to deny salvage and firefighting services to attacked vessels, further raising transit costs and risk. IMF PortWatch recorded just 1 transit on November 22, compared to a pre-crisis baseline of 85 per day. Three US carrier strike groups remain in the Gulf. Goldman Sachs's December Brent forecast of $105 and $140 risk scenario remain in force. OPEC+ meets Saturday.
desk.src: straits.live · Insurance Journal · gCaptain · UKMTO · JMIC · Reuters

desk.name: Corn
desk.m: Dec front-month · up ~6¢ · pre-Thanksgiving holiday trade · fund short-covering · export demand · Black Sea disruption supports
desk.sum: December corn rose approximately 1.3% to 456 cents per bushel on Wednesday in pre-Thanksgiving holiday trade. Fund short-covering and export demand continued to support, with Black Sea maritime disruption maintaining US competitiveness. The rally came despite renewed dollar strength. Corn has been the most resilient grain through November's commodity sell-off. US markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving. Key resistance at 460 cents; support at 450 cents.

desk.name: Wheat
desk.m: Dec SRW · down ~5¢ · pre-Thanksgiving thin trade · mixed grains session · SovEcon: Russia exports 36Mt · Black Sea disruption ongoing
desk.sum: December SRW wheat eased approximately 0.8% to 584 cents per bushel on Wednesday, underperforming corn and soybeans in pre-Thanksgiving holiday trade. Volumes were thin ahead of Thursday's market closure. SovEcon's Russian wheat export estimate of 36 million tonnes — below the USDA forecast — continues to provide structural support. Black Sea disruption remains a factor, but dollar strength and near-term demand softness weighed. Key support at 575 cents; resistance at 590 cents.

desk.name: Soybean
desk.m: January front-month ~$12.36 · up 4¢ · meal support continued · pre-Thanksgiving trade · export demand solid · South American competition
desk.sum: January soybeans edged up approximately 0.3% to 1,236 cents per bushel on Wednesday, modestly higher in pre-Thanksgiving holiday trade. Soybean meal strength continued to provide support. The gain was more muted than corn, reflecting the soybean market's more balanced supply picture. US soybean export commitments remain up approximately 80% year on year. Markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving. Key support at 1,220 cents; resistance at 1,245 cents.

desk.name: Cryptocurrencies
desk.m: ETH $1,640 · BTC broke below $60k · down ~27% in 1 month · Fear & Greed extreme · Nasdaq 100 -2.1% · Dec hike odds ~98% · spot ETF outflows continue
desk.sum: Bitcoin fell approximately 3.2% to $58,500 on Wednesday, breaking below the psychologically important $60,000 level. Ethereum dropped to approximately $1,640. The decline tracked the continued equity sell-off — the Nasdaq 100 fell roughly 2.1%. Bitcoin is now down approximately 27% from a month ago and 33% from its all-time high of $126,198 reached in October 2025. Spot Bitcoin ETF outflows continue. The October PCE data reinforcing December rate-hike expectations added further pressure. The Fear and Greed Index remains in extreme fear territory. Key support at $57,000.

desk.name: LNG
desk.m: JKM held near $29 · TTF ~$28 · HH ~$3.15 · new IRGC mine attacks — LNG carrier struck · Iran blacklists tugboats · QatarEnergy FM continues · Qatar exports at busiest month since war start
desk.sum: The Asian LNG spot JKM holds near $29 per MMBtu, steady despite new IRGC mine attacks in the Strait of Hormuz — including an LNG carrier that caught fire after striking a naval mine on Wednesday. TTF sits near $28 per MMBtu; Henry Hub near $3.15. Iran's move to blacklist 26 tugboats further threatens maritime logistics. Despite the disruptions, Qatar LNG exports hit their busiest month since the start of the Iran war, according to Insurance Journal. QatarEnergy's force majeure extends through at least end-December 2026. The Brent reversal to $94 raises oil-linked LNG contract pricing.
desk.src: S&P Global Platts · Global LNG Hub · Insurance Journal

desk.name: Sulfur
desk.m: FOB Kuwait ~$765 · new IRGC mine attacks add further supply risk · Iran blacklists 26 tugboats · Brent reversal to $94 · 3 US carriers in Gulf
desk.sum: Sulfur remains elevated at approximately $1,200 per tonne CFR Southeast Asia. Wednesday's new IRGC mine attacks — two tankers and an LNG carrier struck — and Iran's blacklisting of 26 tugboats add further supply-side risk to Middle Eastern sulfur logistics. FOB Kuwait holds near $765 (KPC). The Brent crude reversal to $94 supports the petroleum-sulfur production dynamic. Iran's denial of salvage services through the tugboat blacklist complicates maritime operations in the Gulf.

desk.name: Potash
desk.m: BPC India $383 CFR · China benchmark ~$348 · grain mixed — corn +1.3% · Brent reversal raises input costs · Black Sea disruption adds logistics risk
desk.sum: Muriate of potash (MOP) CFR Brazil holds at approximately $358 per tonne. BPC's India contract remains approximately $25 above China's 2026 benchmark at $383 per tonne CFR. Wednesday's grain session was mixed — corn up 1.3%, soybeans up 0.3%, wheat down 0.8% — a neutral signal for fertiliser demand sentiment. Belarus and Russia still account for about 40% of global supply despite Western sanctions. The Brent reversal to $94 on new Hormuz mine attacks modestly raises potash production input costs.

desk.name: Antimony
desk.m: China extends suspension 2 months to Jan 27, 2027 · Rotterdam $18,300–19,000/t · prices stabilised · immediate supply cliff removed · underlying controls remain
desk.sum: Chinese antimony (#1 ingot) holds near ¥92,000 per tonne. China announced a two-month extension of its US-specific export-control suspension, pushing the deadline from November 27 to January 27, 2027 — removing the immediate supply cliff risk. Overseas antimony sits at approximately $18,300–19,000 per tonne in Rotterdam. Market participants note the two-month window is short enough to maintain strategic leverage, and the underlying licensing regimes remain in force during the suspension. If the suspension lapses in January, overseas prices could spike further. China produces close to half of global mined antimony.

desk.name: Gallium & Germanium
desk.m: China extends suspension 2 months to Jan 27, 2027 · China domestic Ga ~$460/kg · 4.5x premium persists · Alcoa Wagerup FID but not producing · underlying controls remain
desk.sum: Gallium holds near $2,100 per kilogram outside China, with Chinese domestic gallium at approximately $460 per kilogram — a roughly 4.5x premium. China announced a two-month extension of its US-specific export-control suspension, pushing the deadline from November 27 to January 27, 2027. The extension removes an immediate supply cliff but the underlying licensing regimes remain in force. China produces approximately 99% of global gallium and 60–80% of germanium. Alcoa's Wagerup gallium refinery has taken FID but is not yet producing. The rolling two-month extensions maintain strategic leverage while avoiding an outright trade rupture.

desk.name: Vanadium
desk.m: Steady at $5.30 · upstream tightness · VRFB adoption timeline uncertain · China-Russia-SA control 90%+ · gallium/germanium deadline extended 2 months
desk.sum: Vanadium pentoxide (V₂O₅) holds at approximately $5.30 per pound in Europe, supported by persistent upstream tightness. China's extension of the gallium, germanium and antimony export-control suspension by two months to January 27, 2027 reduces near-term uncertainty in the broader critical minerals complex. The long-term bull case rests on vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs) for grid-scale energy storage, but adoption timing remains uncertain. China, Russia and South Africa control over 90% of supply.

desk.name: Cocoa
desk.m: Holding near $5,200 · Ivory Coast mid-crop may fall 42–50% YoY · ICE stocks at 2.5-year high · risk-off may ease speculative buying · $5,000 support intact
desk.sum: ICE cocoa holds near $5,200 per tonne, range-bound as competing forces offset each other. Ivory Coast's Sodexam projects 2026/27 output down 21–25% due to El Niño, and Reuters sources suggest the mid-crop could fall 42–50% year on year. Against this, ICE warehouse inventories sit at a 2.5-year high of approximately 3.8 million bags. The broader risk-off mood may ease speculative buying pressure. The $5,000 level has held as strong psychological support. Markets close Thursday for Thanksgiving.

desk.name: Cobalt
desk.m: Continued gradual decline · Rotterdam $16–17/lb · DRC logistics disruption ongoing · NMC-to-LFP shift structural headwind · dollar strength negative
desk.sum: Cobalt is estimated near $32,500 per tonne, continuing a gradual decline. Rotterdam standard-grade cobalt metal sits at $16–17 per pound. The DRC bridge collapse continues to have secondary effects on cobalt logistics. The NMC-to-LFP battery chemistry shift weighs on the structural demand outlook. Wednesday's renewed dollar strength and broader commodity sell-off add further headwind. The market remains in structural surplus.

desk.name: Lithium
desk.m: Continued drift lower from ¥88,000 · structural oversupply persists · Goldman: 444k t global surplus by 2028 · November destocking continues · dollar strength negative
desk.sum: Chinese lithium carbonate continues to drift lower near ¥87,000 per tonne, extending the decline from ¥88,000 earlier in the week. Structural oversupply remains the dominant theme, with Goldman Sachs projecting a 444,000-tonne global surplus by 2028. SMM data shows sustained monthly destocking. The EU's plan to cap Chinese EV imports at 350,000 units per year adds a demand headwind. Supply ramp-ups in Australia and South America continue to outpace demand growth. The ¥85,000 zone represents next major support.

desk.name: Rubber
desk.m: $2.55/kg · SE Asia supply tight · fungal blight ongoing · Brent reversal to $94 raises synthetic rubber costs · auto demand solid
desk.sum: Natural rubber (RSS3) trades near $2,550 per tonne ($2.55/kg), range-bound. Southeast Asian supply remains tight, with Thailand, Indonesia and Malaysia producing 70% of global latex and still affected by Pestalotiopsis fungal leaf blight. Wednesday's Brent reversal to $94 further raises synthetic rubber production costs, tilting the balance toward natural rubber. Auto-sector demand remains solid. The dollar strength that pressured metals had a more muted impact on rubber.

desk.name: Uranium
desk.m: Spot held near $90 · term price $98/lb near record · IAEA: 78 reactors under construction · miners sliding while prices hold · AI demand structural
desk.sum: Uranium spot holds near $90 per pound U₃O₈, with long-term contract prices at $98 per pound — approaching the $100 milestone. Despite spot prices holding above $90 for most of November, uranium miners (URNM ETF) have continued to slide, reflecting rate sensitivity and ETF-driven selling. The IAEA counts 78 reactors under construction worldwide. AI data-centre power demand remains a structural driver. The broader commodity sell-off and dollar strength had limited impact on uranium's supply-driven narrative. Kazatomprom reported strong Q3 results.

desk.name: Rare Earths
desk.m: Pr-Nd prices on the rise per SMM · ex-China NdPr below $110/kg · gallium/germanium deadline extended 2 months · downstream demand sluggish
desk.sum: Neodymium-praseodymium (NdPr) oxide holds at approximately $72 per kilogram domestically in China. SMM reports that Pr-Nd prices are on the rise, with suppliers holding firm and limiting price concessions. Ex-China NdPr prices remain below $110 per kilogram. China's extension of the gallium, germanium and antimony export-control suspension by two months reduces near-term uncertainty in the broader critical minerals complex. Downstream magnetic material orders remain sluggish.

desk.name: Manganese
desk.m: South Africa 37% · Gabon 18% · miners holding firm pricing stance · CIF China flat · metals rout weighs on steel demand outlook
desk.sum: Manganese ore (44% Mn content) trades near $4.40 per dry metric tonne unit CIF China, flat. Miners continue holding a firm pricing stance. South Africa supplies about 37% of global ore and Gabon 18%. Steel production consumes 90% of manganese demand. The broadening base metals rout — with tin down 7.2% and copper at an 11-month low — weighs on steel demand sentiment. The dollar's continued advance is modestly negative for dollar-denominated commodity pricing.

desk.name: Nickel
desk.m: LME 3M ~$15,175 · bucked the base metals rout · touched 1-year low then recovered · Indonesian RKAB uncertainty · global surplus continues
desk.sum: LME nickel edged up 0.5% to $15,175 per tonne on Wednesday, bucking the base metals rout after touching a one-year low. Indonesian RKAB mining quota uncertainty persists — potential tightening provides a floor while the global nickel surplus from Indonesian NPI and HPAL expansions caps upside. Nickel's modest gain contrasted with sharp losses across the rest of the LME complex, suggesting near-term oversold conditions. Key support at $15,000.

desk.name: Tin
desk.m: LME 3M ~$36,710 · plunged 7.2% — 1-year low · Shanghai tin -9.6% intraday · session's worst performer · Myanmar ban still constraining supply · macro headwinds overwhelm
desk.sum: LME tin plunged 7.2% to approximately $36,710 per tonne on Wednesday — its lowest level in a year and the session's worst-performing major commodity. Shanghai tin fell as much as 9.6% intraday, the biggest decline in over a year. The collapse was driven by dollar strength, tariff fears, and continued tech sell-off sentiment, overwhelming structural supply constraints from Myanmar's Wa State mining ban and Indonesian export licensing tightness. The move highlights tin's vulnerability in thin markets during macro-driven sell-offs.

desk.name: Zinc
desk.m: LME 3M ~$3,389 · six-month low · TCs deeply negative · structural deficit intact · dollar strength negative
desk.sum: LME zinc eased 1.5% to approximately $3,389 per tonne on Wednesday, touching a six-month low as the broader base metals rout deepened. Treatment charges remain deeply negative, forcing continued smelter curtailments outside China. The structural supply deficit remains intact despite near-term macro pressure. Zinc is still up approximately 10% year on year. Key support at $3,350.

desk.name: Tungsten
desk.m: Rotterdam APT $2,750 · China FOB $1,845 · Western ~3.5x China · export-control deadline extended 2 months to Jan 27, 2027
desk.sum: European tungsten APT holds at $2,750 per mtu in Rotterdam, while Chinese FOB sits at $1,845 per mtu — Western prices remain roughly 3.5 times Chinese domestic levels. China's extension of the gallium, germanium and antimony export-control suspension by two months to January 27, 2027 reduces near-term disruption risk for the broader critical minerals complex, though the underlying licensing regimes remain in force. The market continues to reflect the fragmentation created by China's export controls.

desk.name: Helium
desk.m: Up 358% YTD · Ras Laffan repair 3–5 years · new IRGC mines struck LNG carrier Wed · Iran blacklists 26 tugboats · Qatar exports at busiest month since war start
desk.sum: Grade-A helium trades near $390 per thousand cubic feet, at critical levels. Wednesday's IRGC mine attack on an LNG carrier in the Strait of Hormuz adds further risk to already-disrupted helium supply logistics from Qatar. Iran's blacklisting of 26 tugboats — denying salvage and firefighting services — further raises the cost of Hormuz transit. However, Qatar LNG exports hit their busiest month since the start of the Iran war, suggesting some supply recovery despite the elevated risk. QatarEnergy's Ras Laffan facility repairs remain estimated at 3–5 years.

desk.name: Phosphate
desk.m: OCP 30% global · DAP $560/t · sulfur cost surge pressuring economics · grains mixed — corn +1.3%
desk.sum: Phosphate rock trades near $120 per tonne FOB Morocco, with Morocco's OCP Group controlling about 30% of global trade. DAP prices sit near $560 per tonne CFR India. The sulfur price surge continues to pressure phosphate production economics. Wednesday's grain session was mixed — corn up 1.3%, soybeans up 0.3%, wheat down 0.8% — a neutral signal for fertiliser demand. The Brent reversal to $94 on new Hormuz mine attacks further reduces the probability of Middle Eastern sulfur supply normalising.

quiz: COMEX gold settled approximately 2.5% lower at $3,474 on Wednesday — the twelfth decline in thirteen sessions — breaking below $3,500 per ounce for the first time since September 2025 as October PCE data reinforced December rate-hike expectations.
Silver rallied 4.9% on Wednesday to $43 per ounce as industrial demand from the solar sector accelerated, lifting the metal above its 50-day moving average for the first time since early November.

Silver actually fell approximately 4.9% to $39 per ounce — continuing the rout alongside gold — as the dollar strengthened further after the October PCE report. Silver has fallen approximately 26% in November.

Brent crude staged a dramatic intraday reversal on Wednesday, initially falling to approximately $87 on supply-surplus fears before surging to $94 after IRGC mines struck two more tankers and an LNG carrier in the Strait of Hormuz.

LME tin rose 7.2% on Wednesday to $42,500 per tonne — its highest level in six months — as Indonesian export restrictions tightened further and Myanmar's Wa State mining ban continued to constrain supply.

LME tin actually fell 7.2% to $36,710 per tonne — its lowest level in a year — as the broader base metals rout deepened. Shanghai tin fell as much as 9.6% intraday, the biggest decline in over a year.
China announced a two-month extension of its US-specific export-control suspension on gallium, germanium and antimony, pushing the deadline from November 27, 2026 to January 27, 2027.

LME copper rose 2% to $5.60 per pound on Wednesday as Chinese physical demand accelerated and the Yangshan premium reached a new record of $400 per tonne, lifting prices above the $12,000 per tonne threshold.
LME copper actually fell approximately 2.2% to $5.26 per pound ($11,596 per tonne) — an 11-month low below $12,000. Copper has fallen approximately 18% in November despite tight physical conditions.

Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority added 26 tugboats to its vessel blacklist on Wednesday, bringing the total to 266 vessels listed for transiting without Tehran's permission — a move analysts said aims to deny salvage and firefighting services to attacked vessels.
Newcastle thermal coal surged 5% to $155 per tonne on Wednesday as the Brent crude reversal to $94 boosted the entire energy complex and winter stockpiling accelerated across Europe and Asia.

Newcastle coal actually eased approximately 1.4% to $145 per tonne. While Brent reversed sharply to $94 on new Hormuz attacks, coal continued its gradual retreat from recent highs as the broader risk-off mood and weaker industrial sentiment weighed.
